title: SDK contract: idempotent cursors, streaming resilience, and retry semantics (Python/TS/Go)
creator: Liam Chen
description: PRD + acceptance criteria to define a cross-language SDK contract for pagination cursors, streaming response resilience and resumability, and standardized retry semantics across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs. The goal is to make migrations safe for customers, ensure observable failure modes, and provide simple, language-native idioms (sync/async iterators, generators, streams) while avoiding per-language behavioral drift.
acceptance_criteria: Cursor contract finalized: CursorV2 is an opaque, base64 compacted JSON string containing {version, model_id, offset, checksum, schema_version} and server-side TTL. SDKs must decode/validate and surface a typed Cursor object in all pagination APIs.

Idempotency token guidance published: SDKs provide a generate_idempotency_token() helper; servers accept client tokens and return stable request identifiers for exactly-once semantics on retryable write-like calls.

Retry policy uniformity: SDKs implement a default retry policy aligned with platform error taxonomy (idempotent: exponential backoff with jitter up to 5 retries; non-idempotent: no automatic retry unless explicit client opt-in with idempotency token).

Streaming resume semantics: streaming endpoints expose a resume token in stream metadata; SDK streaming clients (Python async iterator, TS async generator, Go channel iterator) can resume a stream from the last acknowledged chunk using the resume token without duplicating application-visible units more than once under normal conditions.
Backpressure and flow-control: SDKs expose flow control primitives (max_in_flight / high_watermark) and document recommended defaults; must not buffer unboundedly by default in any language.

Compatibility matrix: integration tests demonstrate forward/backward compatibility across server schema versions (v1, v2) for cursor and resume tokens; tests must run in CI for all three SDK languages before release.
Telemetry hooks: SDKs surface headers for tracing (x-rw-trace-id), emit metrics for retries/restores, and include opt-in debug logs that map retries to user-visible request IDs.
Migration playbook: docs include step-by-step migration guidance for customers using legacy cursors and streaming clients; include rollback steps and expected behaviour under partial upgrades.

Acceptance test suite: end-to-end tests in infra simulate network partitions, duplicated chunks, and server-side cursor rotation to verify SDK behaviors; flakiness threshold < 1% on CI runs over 200 trials.
Documentation and example apps: one sample app per language showing pagination resume, long-running stream resume, and safe retry patterns; included in SDK repo and docs site.
notes: Trade-off: opaque CursorV2 vs human-readable cursor. We chose opaque with embedded version/checksum to allow server evolution without breaking clients and to limit accidental client parsing errors.

Trade-off: server-issued resume tokens reduce client complexity but require server state. We selected stateless resume token design (signed/compact) to minimize server pinned state while allowing token rotation.
Eng feedback: prefer sequence-number + checksum in stream chunks to allow duplicate suppression at client. This increases per-chunk metadata by ~24 bytes but simplifies deduplication in SDKs.
Design note: Python SDK will expose both sync and async iterator surfaces; TS will use async generators; Go will expose a blocking iterator plus context-aware cancellation semantics.

Risk: clients that persist legacy cursors may see failure if server rotates schema aggressively. Mitigation: include schema_version in cursor and server fallback handler for legacy decode path for 6 months post release.

release_notes_snippet: Introduces CursorV2 opaque cursors, standardized retry policy, and streaming resume semantics. SDKs (Python/TS/Go) implement clients to decode CursorV2 and resume streams with signed resume tokens. See migration guide for legacy cursor upgrade path.
